newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin orders end to squabbling over Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin orders end to squabbling over Chechnya.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, cracking the whip from a sanatorium where he is preparing for heart surgery, on Tuesday ordered rivals in the Kremlin and the government to stop bickering over Chechnya.

Yeltsin's spokesman said the ailing Kremlin leader had told Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, security tsar Alexander Lebed and Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov to reach a common position on Chechnya before the start of closed parliamentary hearings later on Tuesday.
The 65-year-old leader, preparing for a heart bypass operation, has told them to stop "verbal duels," his press spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said.
"As far as I know this order has been carried out," Yastrzhembsky told a Kremlin briefing.
"The president is concerned by elements of confrontation on the public political stage...between members of the same team."

Security Council chief Lebed signed a deal with Chechen separatist leaders in August under which Moscow promised to withdraw troops and both sides agreed to postpone a decision on the region's future political status for five years.

But the agreement infuriated other officials, especially Kulikov, who insisted that Chechnya had to remain part of Russia. Lebed holds Kulikov largely responsible for failing to end the conflict and there is no love lost between the two men.
"The president knows all about these verbal duels, accusations and counter-charges," Yastrzhembsky said.
The peace deal is also unpopular among nationalist members of parliament who took advantage of the closed session to heap more abuse on Lebed.
"They tried to lecture me in the Duma. It suddenly turned out that the restoration of peace in Chechnya suits virtually no one," Interfax quoted Lebed as saying after the session.
Lebed, who enjoys huge support among the armed forces, makes no secret of the fact that he would like to succeed Yeltsin but he has already made some powerful enemies.
On Tuesday he lashed out at the Defence Ministry, accusing it of trying to destroy Russia's paratroops by cutting their numbers as part of a package of military reductions.
Interfax quoted Lebed -- who has already warned of a possible army mutiny -- as saying such decisions could cause social unrest and vowed to bring the matter up with Yeltsin.
His words are hardly likely to cement relations with senior officials in the defence ministry, also humiliated over a series of bloody setbacks during the 21-month Chechen conflict.
The separatists have established control over the whole of Chechnya as Russian troops depart and they are replacing Moscow-installed local authorities with their own ones.

Interfax quoted a source in the Russian General Staff as saying the troop withdrawal from the region would be completed by October 21. It was not clear whether this would include Interior Ministry forces stationed in Chechnya.
Moscow plans to keep two brigades, one from the army and another from the interior ministry, in Chechnya permanently.
Interfax news agency said the rebel leadership, which met in southern Chechnya late on Monday, had decided to hold local elections next January.
The meeting had also finalised the line up of a coalition government, formed without Moscow's participation, which would include representatives from different Chechen groups.

The rebels do not recognise pro-Moscow Doku Zavgayev, who was elected Chechen president earlier this year in a poll widely criticised as unfair. Zavgayev's government is not taking part in the peace negotiations.
